stem: In Hirschsprung disease, what is the fundamental pathological defect in the affected segment of bowel?

options.text: Absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses
Necrosis of the intestinal wall due to ischaemia

explanation: Absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses is the key defect in Hirschsprung disease, producing a permanently contracted aganglionic bowel segment and functional obstruction.
rationale: The disease results from failed neural crest cell migration, leaving the affected segment without enteric ganglion cells.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because mucosal hypertrophy is not the primary abnormality in Hirschsprung disease; the problem is aganglionosis of the enteric nervous system.
optionExplanations.B: Correct because Hirschsprung disease is caused by failure of neural crest cells to migrate to the distal bowel, leaving the myenteric and submucosal plexuses without ganglion cells.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because the fundamental problem is not excess inhibitory neurotransmitter production, but absence of the ganglion cells that coordinate normal motility.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because intestinal wall necrosis from ischaemia is not the developmental defect in Hirschsprung disease; it is a separate pathological process.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because mucosal inflammation is not the defining lesion in Hirschsprung disease; the hallmark is absence of enteric ganglion cells.

source.hint: Focus on the specific cellular deficiency within the enteric nervous system.
